impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are directed to an abstract idea under step one of Alice, and whether foreign sales can support a damages award for patent infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also ruled that the district court erred in denying JMOL on damages from foreign sales, rejecting extraterritorial application of patent damages. The enhanced damages and attorneys' fees awards were also set aside due to an improper contempt finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a stronger application of Alice step one to software patents involving emulation and anomaly detection, and from the reinforcement that patent damages cannot be based on foreign sales absent a sufficient domestic nexus.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened eligibility risk, and the ruling limits damages recovery for products sold abroad even when infringing acts have domestic components.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that claims to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for lack of written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The court found that the specification's disclosure of antibody G1, combined with known methods of humanization and the existence of known murine anti-CGRP antibodies, sufficiently supported the genus claims under written description and enablement requirements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more favorable standard for genus claims where the specification discloses representative species and references known methods for producing additional members of the genus, reinforcing protection for biologic drug patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar drug developers face continued patent barriers for biologic therapies, as the ruling sustains broad genus claims covering anti-CGRP antibodies used in lucrative migraine treatments.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to show the asserted trade secrets were not generally known and thus protectable. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity for incorrect inventorship, reasoning that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a rigorous evidentiary standard requiring plaintiffs to prove that asserted trade secrets are not generally known in the industry, reducing the risk of overly broad trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection must ensure robust evidence that their claimed secrets are not generally known, or risk losing both trade secret and related patent claims where the same information underlies inventorship.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights to a licensee but retains the right to sue for infringement (along with other retained rights) has constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to sue third parties for infringement—even after granting an exclusive license for commercialization—possess sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing. The court emphasized that the retained litigation right was not rendered illusory by the license terms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain enforcement rights and maintain standing to sue infringers even after granting broad exclusive licenses, providing flexibility in licensing strategies and patent monetization.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential standing defense where patent owners carefully structure license agreements to retain the right to sue, even when most commercialization rights have been exclusively licensed to a third party.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent infringement claim based on the design of a multicore processor is barred by extraterritoriality when the accused products are manufactured and tested abroad, and whether the district court properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement on extraterritoriality grounds, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether sufficient domestic acts of infringement occurred. The court affirmed the summary judgment on the doctrine of equivalents theory and the striking of certain damages theories for inadequate disclosure in damages contentions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents benefit from the court's narrowing of the extraterritoriality defense where there is evidence of domestic testing, use, or sale of accused products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing operations face continued patent infringement exposure for domestically sold products even when design and fabrication occur abroad, and must carefully manage damages contention disclosures to avoid exclusion of expert theories.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge for summary judgment purposes, and whether source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate deposition witness may testify beyond personal knowledge and that source code consisting of computer commands (as opposed to descriptive comments) is not hearsay. The court rejected the patentee's argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of a prior art device's functionality at the time of sale.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony and source code in proving invalidity, and the ruling confirms that commercial sales of devices embodying claimed features trigger the on-sale bar regardless of whether functionality was publicly disclosed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from prior commercial sales, as the ruling confirms the on-sale bar does not require that the sold device's infringing functionality be expressly disclosed or known to the buyer.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, finding that further analysis was needed under Alice, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents that recited sufficiently concrete implementations. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, upholding the jury's willful infringement verdict.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims that recite specific technical implementations of communications standards may maintain eligibility, and the affirmation of the damages verdict supports robust enforcement of standard-essential and communications technology patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing digital communications standards face ongoing patent infringement liability, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty for patents claiming mathematical optimizations applied to signal constellations.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement, agreeing that 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field (25°C), not at other temperatures. The court also upheld the ruling that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine of equivalents infringement. This decision effectively clears the path for Mylan's generic epoprostenol drug.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from the narrow claim construction of pH-related limitations in pharmaceutical patents, facilitating entry of generic products and reducing barriers from Hatch-Waxman litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower patent protection when claims include measurable parameters like pH, as courts may construe such terms according to standard measurement conditions rather than conditions more favorable to infringement findings.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim for attempted monopolization.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether Tenaris committed inequitable conduct by withholding prior art (the CYMAX Documents) during patent prosecution, and whether that conduct rose to the level of fraud sufficient to support an antitrust attempted monopolization claim. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors asserting Walker Process antitrust claims benefit from the court's recognition that disputed facts about intentional withholding of prior art during patent prosecution can survive summary judgment, keeping alive both unenforceability and antitrust remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased litigation risk when they acquire prior art through asset purchases and later prosecute related patents, as failures to disclose acquired prior art may support both inequitable conduct and antitrust liability.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents covering wearable pulse oximetry devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337, upholding the Commission's domestic industry determination, patent validity rulings, and infringement findings for the Masimo patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement technology. The limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models was sustained.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the medical device and wearable technology space benefit from the affirmation that the ITC can effectively enforce patents against major technology companies importing infringing products, providing a powerful trade remedy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies integrating health-monitoring features into consumer electronics face significant import exclusion risk when those features are covered by third-party patents, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after having missed the statutory deadline for seeking a stay of its original declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for obtaining a mandatory stay under § 1659(a)(2) by voluntarily dismissing its original declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one. The court concluded that allowing such gamesmanship would undermine the statutory framework coordinating parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners pursuing ITC investigations benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate the mandatory stay provision by refiling district court actions, ensuring ITC proceedings can continue without being used as leverage to delay parallel litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day stay deadline lose the ability to obtain a mandatory stay through tactical refiling, potentially forcing them to litigate simultaneously in both the ITC and district court.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy due to the expert's reliance on allegedly flawed methodology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of the patent holder's damages expert report and vacated the resulting summary judgment for Microsoft, finding that the district court applied an overly strict standard in evaluating the expert's methodology. The court held that the issues identified by the district court went to the weight, not admissibility, of the expert testimony.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for damages expert testimony, as the ruling reinforces that methodological disputes generally go to weight rather than admissibility and should be resolved by the factfinder.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face reduced ability to obtain summary judgment based on Daubert exclusion of damages experts, as the Federal Circuit signals that district courts should be cautious in excluding expert testimony on damages methodology grounds.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a third party not sued for patent infringement may file IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against another entity, potentially as a proxy, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded for further proceedings, finding errors in the Board's analysis of the challenged claims. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR, but the decision highlights concerns about potential proxy IPR petitions filed by non-parties to the underlying infringement litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from closer scrutiny of IPR obviousness determinations, and the decision draws attention to potential misuse of the IPR system by entities filing petitions as proxies for time-barred parties.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR petitions to challenge competitor patents face risk that the Board's obviousness findings may be vacated on appeal for analytical shortcomings, prolonging patent disputes and increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a court may correct inventorship under 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) when the omitted coinventor cannot be located, and whether patents are invalid for omission of a coinventor who has not been added.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity for omission of a coinventor (Huang) who could not be located and thus could not be added to the patents. The court upheld the district court's denial of the patentee's motion to judicially correct inventorship under § 256(b), finding that the statute's requirements for correction were not met when the omitted inventor was unavailable.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain a strong invalidity defense when patent owners fail to properly name all coinventors, particularly when joint development with overseas partners makes it difficult to locate and add all contributors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies collaborating with foreign partners on product development face serious patent validity risks if coinventors become unreachable, as the inability to correct inventorship can render the entire patent invalid.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging that PACER fees exceeded statutory authority. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges to jurisdiction, settlement fairness, and the propriety of incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: The decision provides certainty for class action settlements involving government fee overcharges and supports the permissibility of incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives who serve the class's interests.
